paper_title: MatAnyone-E: Sparse Memory Propagation for Efficient High-Resolution Video Matting

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: High-resolution video matting requires preserving fine details, such as hair strands and soft transparency, while maintaining consistency across frames. Memory-based methods achieve strong matting quality by matching current-frame features with information stored from earlier frames, but this process becomes increasingly costly as resolution grows. We present MatAnyone-E, an efficient extension of MatAnyone 2 that focuses computation where it is most needed. Our approach first performs low-resolution propagation to identify uncertain regions that require closer inspection and the memory candidates most relevant to them. It then performs high-resolution matching only for these regions using the selected memory, while reusing low-resolution matching results elsewhere. This strategy reduces both the number of locations requiring detailed matching and the amount of memory searched, while preserving the information needed to produce a complete matte. We further reduce the cost of generating high-resolution mattes with a lightweight decoder designed around measured runtime bottlenecks and trained to reproduce the original decoder's representations. Experiments show that MatAnyone-E maintains matting quality comparable to MatAnyone 2 while achieving an estimated 7.4x inference speedup and reducing peak GPU memory usage to 7.6% of the usage of MatAnyone 2 at 4K. With compilation-enabled inference on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, it reaches 73.07 FPS at 1080p and 28.62 FPS at 4K.

MatAnyone-E (Ours) achieves an estimated 7.4 speedup and 13.1 lower peak GPU memory usage than MatAnyone 2 (Yang et al., 2026), which runs out of memory. By directly processing native 4K inputs, our method preserves finer details and boundaries compared to VideoMaMa (Lim et al., 2026) and SAM2Matting (Shen et al., 2026).

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: High-resolution video matting requires preserving fine details, such as hair strands and soft transparency, while maintaining consistency across frames. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Video matting estimates continuous alpha matte for each frame, enabling foreground subjects to be composited onto new backgrounds. High-resolution applications demand accurate recovery of hair strands, thin structures, and soft transparency, together with temporal consistency to prevent flickering. Meeting these requirements, however, becomes computationally expensive as resolution increases, limiting the practical use of otherwise high-quality methods. Existing video matting methods (Zhang et al., 2025; 2019; Qiao et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2017) address this challenge with different trade-offs. Efficiency-oriented approaches, such as RVM (Lin et al., 2022) and SparseMat (Sun et al., 2023), reduce computation through recurrent temporal modeling or selective high-resolution refinement, but can struggle to preserve fine structures and temporal consistency in challenging scenes. Recent methods such as VideoMaMa (Lim et al., 2026) and SAM2Matting (Shen et al., 2026) leverage generative or segmentation priors, yet their restricted processing resolutions limit the detail they can recover from high-resolution inputs. Memory-based methods, including MatAnyone (Yang et al., 2025) and MatAnyone 2 (Yang et al., 2026), achieve strong matting quality by retrieving information from earlier frames. However, matching currentframe features against stored memory and decoding high-resolution mattes incur substantial computational costs as resolution increases. Although selective matte refinement has been explored, reducing the cost of the underlying temporal memory matching remains distinct challenge. This motivates our central question: how can we preserve the quality of memory-based video matting while avoiding exhaustive high-resolution matching and costly decoding? The main computational bottleneck lies in comparing every current-frame feature with large bank of features stored from earlier frames. Increasing the video resolution enlarges both sets of features, causing the matching cost to grow rapidly even when the number of stored frames remains fixed. Yet detailed matching is not equally important everywhere. The model can rely more on information carried over from the previous frame at some locations, while others depend more strongly on newly retrieved information. This suggests focusing matching computation on locations that require stronger updates from memory. The difficulty is identifying these locations efficiently: the signal indicating how much each location needs an update is obtained only after the expensive matching has already been performed. We address this dilemma with MatAnyone-E, an efficient extension of MatAnyone 2. Our key idea is to use an inexpensive low-resolution propagation pass to guide subsequent computation. This initial pass identifies locations that are likely to benefit most from closer inspection and the memory candidates most relevant to those locations. We then perform matching at the native feature resolution only between these selected locations and memory candidates, reusing the upsampled low-resolution matching results elsewhere. Selecting locations alone would still require searching the entire memory bank; selecting relevant memory as well reduces both sources of matching cost. The resulting dense matching output is then used for downstream alpha prediction. Beyond memory matching, producing the high-resolution alpha matte remains substantial computational cost. We therefore develop lightweight decoder guided by measured runtime bottlenecks, since reducing arithmetic operations alone does not necessarily improve inference speed. We train this decoder through knowledge distillation from the original decoder to preserve matting quality. Together, selective memory matching and efficient decoding address the two main sources of highresolution inference cost. Experiments show that MatAnyone-E maintains matting quality comparable to MatAnyone 2 while substantially improving inference efficiency. At 4K resolution, our complete model achieves an estimated 7.4 inference speedup and reduces peak GPU memory usage to 7.6% of MatAnyone 2. Compared with prior methods, MatAnyone-E provides stronger balance between matting quality and inference efficiency at high resolutions.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Video Matting. Video matting methods address the coupled challenges of alpha-detail recovery, temporal consistency, and computational efficiency. RVM (Lin et al., 2022) uses recurrent feature aggregation for real-time human video matting. SparseMat (Sun et al., 2023) exploits spatio-

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: temporal sparsity for selective high-resolution refinement, while µMatting (Chen et al., 2026) targets 4K matting with selective refinement and introduces the αMatte4K dataset. These efficiencyoriented methods (Ke et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2021) highlight efficient temporal modeling and selective refinement as important strategies for high-resolution matting. Another line of work (Li et al., 2024a; Lin et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024b) leverages external guidance and pretrained priors. FTP-VM (Huang & Lee, 2023) jointly models trimap propagation and matting. MaGGIe (Huynh et al., 2024) combines transformer attention and sparse convolution for maskguided instance matting. Matting Anything 2 (Zhang et al., 2026a) uses separate memory pathways for masks and trimaps. SAM2Matting (Shen et al., 2026) connects video tracking (Ravi et al., 2025; Carion et al., 2026) with dedicated matting heads. GVM (Ge et al., 2025) exploits video diffusion priors (Blattmann et al., 2023), while VideoMaMa (Lim et al., 2026) leverages generative priors to convert segmentation masks into alpha mattes and train SAM2-Matte. Closely related to our work, MatAnyone (Yang et al., 2025) introduces region-adaptive memory fusion for stable target-assigned video matting. MatAnyone 2 (Yang et al., 2026) further improves matting through learned quality evaluation, large-scale real-world data curation, and reference-frame training. We build on this memory-based framework and focus on reducing its high-resolution inference cost. Whereas methods such as SparseMat and µMatting reduce computation through selective matte refinement, reducing the cost of the underlying temporal memory matching remains distinct challenge. Efficient Video Object Segmentation. Memory-based video object segmentation (VOS) provides foundation for temporal information propagation. STCN (Cheng et al., 2021) improves efficiency through shared frame correspondences and distance-based affinity. XMem (Cheng & Schwing, 2022) combines sensory, working, and long-term memories to control memory growth over long videos. Cutie (Cheng et al., 2024) augments pixel-level memory reading with object-level queries for more robust target representations. SAM 2 (Ravi et al., 2025) extends promptable segmentation to videos through streaming memory attention. These methods highlight the importance of memory representation and efficient memory access for temporal propagation. Recent work further reduces the cost of memory-based VOS. EfficientTAM (Xiong et al., 2025) combines lightweight plain ViT encoder with spatially compressed memory attention. EdgeTAM (Zhou et al., 2025) compresses frame memories using 2D Spatial Perceiver with global and patch-level queries, supported by knowledge distillation. Efficient-SAM2 (Zhang et al., 2026b) introduces object-aware window routing and sparse memory retrieval to reduce redundant computation. These approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of memory compression and selective computation for efficient temporal propagation. Our work extends this efficiency perspective to high-resolution video matting by using uncertainty estimated from inexpensive low-resolution propagation to determine where native-resolution matching is needed, together with query-dependent memory selection.

As illustrated in Fig. 2(c), both the original and lightweight decoders progressively upsample features through four stages, increasing the spatial resolution from 1/16 to 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, and finally the full input resolution. While the original decoder uses dense convolutions throughout, simply replacing them with lower-FLOP depthwise-separable convolutions does not consistently reduce latency across stages. In particular, at higher spatial resolutions, the reduction in arithmetic cost is increasingly offset by lower arithmetic intensity and increased memory-access overhead, so fewer FLOPs do not necessarily translate into faster execution. We therefore adopt different lightweight designs at different stages. For the 1/16 1/8 and 1/8 1/4 stages, we use depthwise 3 3 convolution followed by pointwise 1 1 convolution. For the 1/4 1/2 and 1/2 1 stages, where reducing memory traffic becomes more important, we retain dense convolutions but reduce their channel widths. This stage-wise design follows the measured runtime behavior of each stage rather than applying single lightweight block throughout the decoder. Detailed stage-wise profiling and analysis are provided in Appendix D. Feature Distillation. While these lightweight designs reduce inference cost, they might limit the decoders representation capacity. To prevent this, we apply feature distillation during training, so that the intermediate representations learned by the original decoder are preserved. Specifically, we use the MatAnyone 2 decoder as frozen teacher and the lightweight decoder as the student. We compare MatAnyone-E with RVM (Lin et al., 2022), FTP-VM (Huang & Lee, 2023), MaGGIe (Huynh et al., 2024), GVM (Ge et al., 2025), MatAnyone (Yang et al., 2025), VideoMaMa (Lim et al., 2026), SAM2Matting (Shen et al., 2026), and its baseline, MatAnyone 2 (Yang et al., 2026). Table 1 reports results on three video matting benchmarks. Compared with MatAnyone 2, MatAnyone-E largely preserves matting quality: MAD differs by at most 0.04 and dtSSD by at most 0.07 across all three datasets. It also achieves lower MSE on VideoMatte (0.25 vs. 0.28), YouTubeMatte (0.45 vs. 0.50), and CRGNN (1.85 vs. 2.00). Compared with recent methods, MatAnyone-E outperforms SAM2Matting across all reported metrics and datasets, and achieves lower MAD and MSE than VideoMaMa across all three benchmarks.

Figure 3 compares MatAnyone-E with MatAnyone, VideoMaMa, and SAM2Matting on representative challenging examples. In regions containing fine hair and soft boundaries, MatAnyone-E recovers cleaner and more complete alpha structures with fewer missing or blurred details. It also better preserves challenging foreground structures, such as hands and objects interacting with the subject, while maintaining accurate local boundaries. The advantage becomes more evident at 4K resolution, where MatAnyone-E processes the native-resolution input and preserves finer hair structures than methods operating at restricted processing resolutions. As shown in Table 3, both Sparse Memory Propagation (SMP) and the lightweight decoder (LD) improve inference efficiency while maintaining comparable matting quality. Compared with the MatAnyone 2 baseline, SMP reduces latency from 73.53 ms to 44.18 ms and peak GPU memory from 5.47 GB to 2.78 GB, while LD reduces them to 66.61 ms and 4.35 GB, respectively. Combining both components gives the full MatAnyone-E model, achieving 37.59 ms latency, 26.6 FPS, and 1.66 GB peak memory. Query-Selection Strategy. As shown in Table 4, we compare different strategies for selecting query locations for HR matching using the MatAnyone 2 checkpoint. The dense baseline performs HR matching at all query locations, while LR only uses only the LR readout without further HR matching. Under similar HR query budget, uncertainty-guided selection achieves better matting quality than uniform sampling and alpha-boundary selection, while maintaining comparable latency. This supports using the uncertainty estimated from LR propagation to identify locations that benefit most from HR matching.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented MatAnyone-E, an efficient framework for high-resolution video matting. Our key insight is that dense high-resolution memory matching is largely redundant: only subset of query locations requires precise retrieval, and only subset of memory is relevant to them. By restricting native-resolution matching to selected querymemory pairs and reusing the upsampled lowresolution readout elsewhere, Sparse Memory Propagation substantially reduces the cost of temporal memory retrieval. lightweight decoder further reduces high-resolution decoding cost through profiling-guided design and feature distillation. MatAnyone-E preserves the strong matting quality of MatAnyone 2 while achieving an estimated 7.4 inference speedup and 13.1 lower peak GPU memory at 4K. We believe selective high-resolution computation offers practical direction for scaling memory-based video matting to high resolutions.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: the coarsest grid contains no more than spatial locations. This produces sequence of scales (s0, s1, . . . , sL), where sL = 1 corresponds to the native memory-feature resolution. Propagation first operates densely at the coarsest level. The resulting memory readout is used to estimate uncertainty, and only query locations whose uncertainty exceeds the threshold are propagated at the next finer level. For these selected queries, we further restrict matching to subset of memory candidates identified from the coarse affinities. Specifically, memory candidates are ranked according to their maximum affinity to the selected query regions, and only the top ρ fraction is retained. Sparse propagation is then performed between the selected queries and retained memory candidates. The refined readouts replace the corresponding regions of the upsampled coarse result, while the remaining locations directly retain the coarse prediction. This process is repeated until the native memory-feature resolution is reached. Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete procedure. When only single refinement level is required, the algorithm reduces to the formulation described in the main paper. For all 4K experiments reported in the main paper, we consistently use 4 2 1 propagation schedule with the spatial budget set to = 4096.

sections.content: B.1 RUNTIME BOTTLENECKS OF MATANYONE 2 Table 5: Per-module runtime breakdown of MatAnyone 2 across resolutions and memory-bank sizes. Runtime is reported in milliseconds per frame. The 4K result with five memory frames is estimated because the full configuration exceeds GPU memory. Module 1080p (mem=5) 1440p (mem=5) 4K (mem=2) 4K (mem=3) 4K (mem=5, est.) Encoder Memory Propagation Object Transformer Decoder Value Encoder Others Total latency 9.12 34.35 7.56 17.59 4.54 0.73 73. 15.81 115.94 8.33 30.37 7.53 0.85 178.83 34.11 314.58 13.86 67.21 16.22 1.25 445.10 34.10 469.65 13.91 67.22 16.22 1.34 600. 34.11 779.80 14.01 67.22 16.22 1.51 911.00 To better understand the source of high-resolution inference cost, we profile MatAnyone 2 at the module level across input resolutions and memory-bank sizes. As shown in Table 5, memory propagation increasingly dominates runtime as the spatial resolution grows, accounting for 46% of the total runtime at 1080p and 65% at 1440p. At 4K, the bottleneck becomes substantially more pronounced: increasing the memory bank from two to five frames raises the memory-propagation cost from 314.58 ms to an estimated 779.80 ms, while the runtime of the remaining modules remains nearly unchanged. Consequently, the total per-frame latency increases from 445.1 ms to approximately 911 ms. The decoder is the second-largest high-resolution component, but unlike memory propagation, its cost is largely independent of the memory-bank size. These results identify dense memory propagation as the primary runtime bottleneck of MatAnyone 2 at high resolution. B.2 COMPONENT-WISE EFFICIENCY ANALYSIS We next isolate the contribution of each component to inference efficiency. Table 6 progressively introduces query pruning (QP), memory pruning (MP), the lightweight decoder (LD), and compilation on top of MatAnyone 2. Query pruning provides the largest reduction in memory-propagation cost, with increasingly pronounced gains at higher resolutions. At 4K, QP reduces latency from 909.09 ms to 157.67 ms and peak memory from 79.69 GB to 10.10 GB. Memory pruning further restricts matching along the memory dimension. At 8K, adding MP on top of QP reduces latency from 1174.04 ms to 578.00 ms and peak memory from 45.79 GB to 39.87 GB. The lightweight decoder provides complementary reduction in dense high-resolution computation. At 4K, it reduces latency from 143.55 ms to 123.46 ms, peak memory from 10.18 GB to 6.08 GB, and computational cost from 3.77 to 2.72 TFLOPs per frame. Compilation further improves runtime without changing the reported FLOPs or model parameters, reducing the 4K latency from 123.46 ms to 73.53 ms. Overall, the results show that the main efficiency gains of MatAnyone-E come from reducing dense memory matching, while memory pruning becomes increasingly beneficial at very high resolutions and the lightweight decoder provides complementary savings in dense decoding. B.3 RESOLUTION DEPENDENCE OF SPARSE MEMORY PROPAGATION Sparse Memory Propagation relies on low-resolution uncertainty and affinities to guide query and memory selection, and its effectiveness therefore depends on the spatial resolution of the underlying feature grid. At lower input resolutions, the downsampled feature map can become too coarse to reliably localize uncertain regions or distinguish relevant memory candidates, limiting the benefit of selective matching.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: This effect is particularly noticeable for query pruning. As shown in Table 6, its efficiency gain becomes more pronounced as the input resolution increases: the benefit is relatively modest at 1080p, becomes clearer at 1440p, and grows substantially at 4K and 8K. Memory pruning shows similar resolution-dependent trend. Its additional gain is limited at 1080p and 1440p, but becomes much more significant at 8K, where the memory dimension is considerably larger. These results indicate that Sparse Memory Propagation is most beneficial at high spatial resolutions, while its advantage can be limited when the low-resolution feature grid becomes too small.

sections.title: C ANALYSIS OF MEMORY PRUNING
sections.content: Table 7: Recall of dense memory matching under different memory pruning ratios. Keep ratio KV retained Recall count Recall weight Top-1 hit 5% 10% 15% 20% 30% 50% 4.94% 9.84% 14.76% 19.71% 29.67% 49.70% 0.8318 0.9503 0.9805 0.9908 0.9977 0.9999 0.8333 0.9508 0.9807 0.9909 0.9977 0. 0.9363 0.9879 0.9962 0.9985 0.9997 1.0000 We further analyze how well the pruned memory set preserves the candidates selected by dense matching. Table 7 reports the retained KV ratio together with three recall statistics under different pruning ratios. Here, recall count measures the fraction of dense-matching candidates retained after pruning, recall weight measures the fraction of their affinity mass retained, and Top-1 hit measures the fraction of queries whose highest-affinity memory candidate is preserved. The relevant memory candidates are highly concentrated. Retaining only 10% of the memory bank already recovers approximately 95% of the dense-matching candidates and weights, while preserving the original top-1 match for 98.8% of queries. At our default keep ratio of 15%, the retained memory set preserves 98.1% of both candidate count and affinity weight, with top-1 hit rate of 99.6%. Increasing the keep ratio beyond 15% yields diminishing improvements in recall. These results indicate that coarse affinities provide reliable signal for identifying query-relevant memory candidates. We therefore use 15% keep ratio in our experiments as trade-off between retaining relevant memory and pruning redundant memory before high-resolution matching.

This motivates us to adopt stage-dependent lightweight design rather than uniform operator replacement across all decoder stages. For the compute-bound lower-resolution stages, we use depthwise-separable convolutions to reduce arithmetic cost. For the high-resolution stages, where memory traffic becomes increasingly important, we instead reduce channel width while retaining dense convolutions. Together, these choices reduce decoder cost while accounting for the different computational characteristics of individual stages.

sections.title: E EFFICIENCY ACROSS GPU ARCHITECTURES
sections.content: To evaluate the efficiency of MatAnyone-E across hardware platforms, we benchmark it on five GPUs spanning consumer, professional, and datacenter classes. Table 9 reports throughput and peak GPU memory across four resolutions, with and without compilation. Across all tested GPUs, MatAnyone-E exhibits consistent scaling trends as the input resolution increases. Compilation further improves throughput and reduces peak memory across devices. At 4K, the compiled model reaches 9.0 FPS on an RTX 3090, 19.1 FPS on an RTX 5090, 9.4 FPS on an RTX A6000, 13.6 FPS on an A800-SXM4-80GB, and 28.6 FPS on an H200 NVL. These results show that the efficiency characteristics of MatAnyone-E remain consistent across wide range of GPU architectures.

sections.title: F ADDITIONAL QUALITATIVE RESULTS
sections.content: Additional Qualitative Comparison. Figure 5 provides additional qualitative comparisons at 2K and 4K resolutions, complementing the examples shown in the main paper.

sections.content: Figure 6: Comparison with MatAnyone 2 at high resolution. MA2 denotes MatAnyone 2. (a) Comparison at 2K input resolution, where MatAnyone-E achieves detail accuracy comparable to that of MA2. (b) Comparison at 4K input resolution, where MA2 is evaluated at 2K because its full 4K configuration exceeds available GPU memory, while MatAnyone-E directly processes the native 4K input. As result, MA2 gives blurry details due to direct upsampling, and sometimes makes semantic mistakes when differentiating foreground from background. Comparison with MatAnyone 2. Figure 6 provides additional comparisons with the direct baseline. At 2K, MatAnyone-E preserves finer hair structures, while the advantage becomes more apparent for 4K inputs, where MatAnyone-E can directly process the native resolution. Additional High-Resolution Results. Figure 7 presents qualitative results on real-world 4K sequence with complex curly hair. Despite the dense and irregular hair boundaries, MatAnyoneE preserves fine foreground structures across frames. We further demonstrate MatAnyone-E on three additional high-resolution sequences covering diverse scenarios: multi-person scenes  (Fig. 8)  and AI-generated content  (Fig. 9)  . These results illustrate the ability of MatAnyone-E to maintain detailed foreground boundaries and temporally consistent matting results across different types of high-resolution content.
